body.heading: You are an ecosystem
paragraphs: Your body is home to trillions of microorganisms — bacteria, fungi and viruses — collectively called the microbiome. They live on your skin, in your mouth and above all in your gut. By cell count they are roughly as numerous as your own cells: you are about half microbial.

Each body site has its own community, adapted to local conditions like a biome. The dry forearm, the oily forehead and the warm, dark gut host quite different species, and your mix is as individual as a fingerprint.

body.heading: What the tenants do for you
paragraphs: Gut microbes earn their keep. They digest fibres your own enzymes cannot touch, releasing nutrients and producing vitamins, including vitamin K and some B vitamins. They also crowd out harmful germs simply by occupying the space and food first.

They tutor the immune system too. Exposure to the right microbes early in life helps the immune system learn what to attack and what to tolerate — one reason scientists link very sterile childhoods with higher rates of allergy.

body.heading: Handle with care
paragraphs: The community is resilient but not invincible. Antibiotics, taken for an infection, also kill helpful gut bacteria, and the community can take weeks to recover — sometimes allowing troublemakers to bloom in the gap.

Your microbiome is assembled from birth onwards, shaped by diet, environment and the people and animals around you. Feeding it fibre — vegetables, beans, whole grains — feeds the species that feed you back. Researchers are now testing whether carefully chosen microbes can be given as medicine, seeding or restoring communities that have gone wrong. It is a young science, and its boldest claims are still being tested.

takeaway: The microbiome is the community of trillions of microbes living on and in the body; they aid digestion, make vitamins and help train the immune system.
